paragraphs.heading: Drifters of the water
paragraphs.text: Plankton are living things that drift in water, or in air, and cannot push themselves against a current or the wind. The name comes from a Greek word for a drifter or wanderer. A single one is called a plankter. Some, like jellyfish, can swim slowly, but generally not fast enough to beat the currents.

paragraphs.heading: Defined by lifestyle, not family
paragraphs.text: The group is set by where an organism lives and how well it moves, not by its family tree. So plankton come from all the major kingdoms of life, from microscopic bacteria, archaea and algae up to jellyfish and ctenophores. Swimmers strong enough to fight a current are called nekton instead, and creatures living on the deep sea floor are called benthos. Organisms floating on or near the surface are called neuston.

paragraphs.heading: Four ways to eat
paragraphs.text: Plankton were traditionally split into two feeding groups. Phytoplankton, such as diatoms and cyanobacteria, make their own food, while zooplankton, such as copepods and radiolarians, eat other living things the way animals do. Research has shown that many single cells, including many dinoflagellates, both photosynthesize and swallow food, so a third group, the mixoplankton, is now recognised. A fourth group, the decomposers, includes bacterioplankton, microscopic fungi and viruses, which recycle nutrients so other plankton can use them as food again.

paragraphs.heading: Small but essential
paragraphs.text: Plankton smaller than about a millimetre keep aquatic ecosystems healthy and balanced. Phytoplankton produce roughly half of Earth's oxygen and play a major role in locking away carbon. Marine microorganisms may make up 70 to 90 percent of the living mass in the ocean, and they largely drive the biological pump, which pulls carbon dioxide from the air and sends carbon down to deeper water. Taken together, plankton are the foundation of the marine food web, feeding species from forage fish to baleen whales.

paragraphs.heading: Light first, then nutrients
paragraphs.text: How many plankton live in a place changes from region to region, with depth and with the seasons. Light is the main reason. Nearly all plankton ecosystems are powered by sunlight, which keeps almost all of their production in surface waters and in places and seasons with plenty of light. Nutrients come second. Much of the tropical and subtropical ocean has lots of light but little nitrate, phosphate and silicate, so production there is relatively low.

paragraphs.heading: Iron from desert dust
paragraphs.text: Some ocean regions hold plenty of the main nutrients and are still unproductive. They are short of the micronutrient iron, and adding it can set off blooms of phytoplankton. Iron mostly reaches the ocean as dust settling on the sea surface. So, oddly, waters next to dry, barren land are often rich in phytoplankton, as in the eastern Atlantic, where trade winds carry dust from the Sahara.

paragraphs.heading: Lifelong drifters and visitors
paragraphs.text: Holoplankton spend their whole lives as plankton; most algae, copepods and salps are examples. Meroplankton drift for only part of their lives, usually as larvae, and later either swim freely or live on the sea floor. Most fish, along with sea urchins, starfish, crustaceans and marine worms, start out this way as larvae.
